X17 at n_TOF: when the scintillators recover from the γ-flash

Every n_TOF beam pulse starts with an intense flash of γ-rays that blinds the scintillators for a moment. How soon can they be trusted again, and which neutron energies does that leave us?

1

The set-up, seen from above

The neutron beam comes out of the page and hits a small cell of ³He gas in the middle.

A neutron captured there can produce an electron–positron pair (red lines). Each one crosses, in order:

a Micromegas tracker (its direction)

a wall of SiPM-read bars

two plastic scintillator bars

a liquid scintillator

The three scintillators tell us when the particle passed and how much energy it left.

2

One beam pulse: what the scintillators record in the first 10 µs

The flash drives every scintillator to its limit; the wall is switched off for the first ~0.7 µs. What follows is the tail of the flash plus a rain of real particles from the beam. The green lines mark when each one can be read again; the rest of these slides show how we decided that.

3

How we test it: two kinds of beam pulse

n_TOF alternates full- and half-intensity proton pulses on the same target

full-intensity beam pulse · 8.5×10¹² protons

half-intensity beam pulse · ~4×10¹² protons

Half the protons give half the flash and half as many particles, but the same kinds of particles at each moment after the flash.

So at any given time, a detector that has recovered sees the same mix of signal sizes after both pulses. If the bigger flash still disturbs it, the two mixes differ.

4

What we compare: how often each signal size occurs

full-intensity beam pulse

half-intensity beam pulse (sizes rescaled to match)

Each curve counts the real signals recorded in one short time window. The half-intensity signals are stretched in size to line up with the full-intensity ones, since a detector may give smaller signals after a bigger flash. On the plastic, 0.6 µs after the flash, the two shapes already agree. The wall still disagrees at 1.8 µs and agrees by 3.5 µs.

5

Shape mismatch between full- and half-intensity pulses, against time

For each moment after the flash we stretch the half-intensity curve to fit the full-intensity one as well as possible, and record how far apart they still are: 0 % means identical shapes. Green band: within 10 %, which we count as the same. The liquids stay 10–20 % apart even long after the flash, so this test cannot clear them.

6

Signal size: the plastics give ~3× smaller signals at first, back to normal by ~10 µs

full-intensity beam pulse

half-intensity beam pulse

possible range

The flash leaves the plastic photomultipliers giving smaller signals for a while. We can see particles from 0.8 µs, but only from 2.0 µs can we measure by how much their signals are reduced, so energies measured before then are uncertain. The SiPM wall shows no such loss.

7

How often a particle crossing the scintillator is seen

full-intensity beam pulse

half-intensity beam pulse

not recovered yet

The particles we care about, the X17 electron and positron, are fast and leave a characteristic amount of energy, like the cosmic muons we use as a reference (a "MIP", minimum-ionizing particle). Since that amount varies from particle to particle, we take the real spread measured with cosmic muons and ask what fraction would still be picked out of the busy signal after the flash.

8

How precisely a particle is measured

full-intensity beam pulse

half-intensity beam pulse

not recovered yet

size uncertain

How far off a typical measurement of a MIP's energy and arrival time is, against time after the flash. Measured by adding artificial signals of known size and time to the real recorded traces of thousands of beam pulses and seeing how well they come back, corrected for the signal-size loss measured from the real data. The plastics measure time to well under a nanosecond; the wall is held back by the many other particles arriving at the same time.
